The Five Senses. Sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are the classical categorization of human sensory systems through which perception of the external world is mediated. This taxonomy was established in ancient philosophy and refined by modern physiology, reflecting the primary channels through which sensory organs transmit chemical and physical stimuli to the brain for conscious and unconscious processing.

Vision is the perception of light and color via photoreceptors called rods and cones in the retina, and for most humans it is the most informational sense. Hearing is the detection of sound waves via the cochlea and hair cells in the inner ear, and it is crucial for communication and spatial awareness. Taste is the detection of chemical compounds in food and liquid via taste buds on the tongue, sensitive to sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami. Smell is the detection of volatile chemical molecules via olfactory receptors in the nasal mucosa, and it is the sense most directly linked to memory and emotion. Touch, or tactile sensation, is the detection of pressure, temperature, and pain via mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors distributed across the skin.

Aristotle codified the classical five in ancient Greek philosophy. Though modern neuroscience has since identified additional sensory modalities like balance and proprioception, the classical five remain the foundation of sensory understanding in philosophy, medicine, and everyday language.
